Library_Story__c: Nesbitt Park is the gathering point for the community known as Governors Bridge in mid-town Toronto. The concept of a little free library is consistent with the community feel of this park and so in the fall of 2013, an initiative was launched to obtain City permission to install it and obtain and decorate the library itself. Chris Fraser organized logistics of municipal approvals and spear-headed public relations. Bill Wrigley, a well-known champion of little free libraries in the Greater Toronto Area built the box. Jacqueline Jordan stenciled ferns and literary quotations all over the library and organized the kick-off. The little free library, branch # 1832, was officially launched on January 21, 2014 in -30 degree Celsius (-22 F) weather which was tempered by a donation of hot chocolate by the manager of Tim Hortons (1840 Bayview Ave). The launch took place, not long after sunrise around 8:15 am to coincide with gathering for the "walking school bus". The park is the weekday morning meeting point where local school children are dropped off by parents and then walk together with designated adults on the "walking school bus" the rest of the way up to Bennington Heights Elementary School. Also, at the park, a community picnic takes place every September- dads wheel their barbeques up the street and everyone donates food (odd number houses donate desserts and even numbered houses donate salads). Games take place and a good time is had by all. In the winter, local parents put up and maintain a rink so the children can skate outside for a couple of months. Nesbitt Park is the Governors Bridge "town square" and how appropriate to have a library in the centre of town.

Library_Story__c: I was gifted my LFL when I retired after 35 years as an elementary/middle school teacher. My favourite role was as a teacher-librarian of more than 20 years. Name: LIB-000101194
Library_Story__c:
I fell in love with Free Little Libraries in Toronto, visiting one in Parkdale each time I was near, and finding some life changing reads in it. Out of a desire to be comfortable working with power tools, make something with my hands and keep the love of Little Free Libraries in my world, I spent the summer and fall of 2023 building this one myself and loving every minute! I’m a mama of two young ones, a visual artist and huge lover of books. I am very interested in psychology, spirituality, nature, memoirs, child rearing and kids books! So, I try to keep the library in these realms and at the same time I love to see how it naturally evolves with the welcomed community input :).

I constructed the library solidly to withstand the weather, with a cedar roof and cedar inside to give visitors a yummy smell when they open the door, and to deter any bugs. Its painted black to match our home, but with a cedar thatched roof to give it that cottage-y cosy feel. I hope you enjoy!

Name: LIB-000188846
Library_Story__c:
Picture a small, weathered wooden box at the edge of a quiet suburban street—at first glance just a typical Free Little Library. But as you get closer, it feels… off. The paint is a faded deep black and red, chipped in places, with black vine-like tendrils creeping up the sides as if something is trying to break through from underneath. Above the door, hand-painted in uneven letters, it reads: “The Bookside Down”—but one or two letters are slightly reversed, like they’ve slipped into the Upside Down.
The the sides are strung with tiny multicolored Christmas lights, some dim, some blinking erratically even in daylight. Between them are alphabet letters, with bulbs positioned over them—an unmistakable nod to Joyce’s wall. Occasionally, if you open the door, you can hear a faint crackling sound, like distant radio static or a Demogorgon growl.

It has since immigrated with me to Montréal, Canada and the Gay Village. The local queer community rallied after it was emptied and refilled with bibles on the first night. Within hours of hearing about this people came to refill it with a new colorful and diverse selection!

I found an old cabinet and my neighbour, Paul, thought a copy of my house would be fun so he added the roof, "windows" and "doors" to the sides. I painted plants and paths all around. It's a work in progress.

Our goal is to keep the free library filled with books to share.

As I chatted with neighbours while we were all home during these past few months due to the pandemic, a neighbour offered to use scrap wood from everyone's garage to build one for me. I then painted with the paint I had left from my front door and voila, the neighbourhood built our first LFL that has already gained a steady stream of regular 'hood users!

Kellie Diguangco is a Literacy advocate, lover of children's books, imagination aficionado, instructor, and mom of 4. Kellie knew Granville Island would make a unique home for a Little Free Library and hopes to continue to spread the love of Literacy to children everywhere.
